source.title: Residential Interior Design - A Guide to Planning Spaces

coverage_audit.notes: Full Chapter 1 processed as rendered pages plus extracted text: printed pages 1-28, input pages 1-28, master pages 15-42. Every page was reviewed for text, tables, figures, captions, legends, callouts and dimension lines. Master page numbers were derived from the input file name suffix 15-42, which matches the page count exactly; this derivation is flagged in the review queue. Three internal inconsistencies were found and preserved rather than corrected: the 2015 dwelling area metric equivalency (245 versus 254 m2), the Figure 1-6 caption metric value 118 mm against the dimension line 1118 mm, and the IRC E3901.2.1 metric value 1289 mm against 6 ft. No page was unreadable.

top_findings.why_useful: IRC minimum habitable room area of 70 sq ft (6.5 m2) with no plan dimension under 7 ft (2134 mm) is the hardest floor available for generated room footprints.
Sloped ceiling rule turns ceiling height into a usable-area computation rather than a single height test, which matters for attic and loft rooms.
Glazing at 8 percent and openable ventilation at 4 percent of floor area tie window sizing directly to room area.
Hall personal-casual band of 0.5 to 1.2 m is the proxemic target for sizing conversation groups, and the source explicitly links casual interaction to it.
Shows that a nominal 32 in door yields only 30 in of clear passage, forcing an explicit separation of door leaf width from clear width in the vocabulary.

chapter_summary.notes: Chapter 1 is an introductory chapter, so a large share of its content is conceptual: proxemics, territory and privacy theory, sustainability policy, lighting fundamentals and drawing conventions. Hard numeric material clusters in three places: IRC requirements for habitable rooms, accessibility and visitability heights and widths, and Hall proxemic distance bands. All records are SOURCE_CANDIDATE only. HARD_CANDIDATE was used sparingly and only for cited IRC code minima whose applicability gate (habitable space, one- and two-family dwellings, 2015 edition) is explicit in the source; every recommendation, preference or typical value was kept below that level.
